blockers.quote: The fact lands on you: anything found in the soil worth more than ten rupees goes to the Collector, or a year in prison, under an Act from 1878 (not verified yet); then one more, a finder beats everyone except the owner (Armory v Delamirie, not verified yet), and the owner's family is in the lane outside.
blockers.why: Scope and legal error: Armory v Delamirie (1722) is an English common law ruling concerning lost chattels found in public places; it does not apply to treasure buried in soil in India, which is governed by the Indian Treasure Trove Act 1878 (and under common law, chattels embedded in private soil belong to the landowner). Additionally, under the 1878 Act, treasure found in soil exceeding ten rupees must be reported and deposited with the Collector for inquiry; failure to report risks forfeiture and up to a year in prison, rather than an automatic forfeiture to the Collector.
blockers.fix: Drop Armory v Delamirie and ground the belief-breaking fact strictly in the Indian Treasure Trove Act of 1878: finding treasure in the soil worth more than ten rupees requires reporting and depositing it with the Collector, with failure to report punishable by up to a year in prison (needs a source).

blockers.fix: Scope the finding to US military records (needs a source): 'then a lost hydrogen bomb—one of six the US military never recovered—'.
